SHAPE_FIELDS: Small satellite craters round the rim.
Ragged patches of throw-out beyond the rim.
How much the edge face widens and narrows along the outline (on a carried cross-section, every width of it).
Lean (back length over face; 0: the shape's own)

How much longer the slope toward the lean side runs than the one away from it (100: the same both sides). 0 keeps what the shape does on its own: a hill's long back, a plateau's wider faces toward north, no lean on the rest.
How far the outline strays from the line you drew, as a share of what roughness gives this kind (100: as it is; 0: a clean outline).
How much the shape widens and narrows along its outline, as a share of what roughness gives it (100: as it is; 0: an even width).
How much the height wanders along the shape, as a share of what roughness gives it (100: as it is; 0: an even crest).
The side the shape leans toward, the long gentle slope: a map direction or a side of the line you draw (a ridge's steep face is the opposite side).
Interlocking land fingers and inlets along the shore.
Width of the dry bank from the waterline to the level ground, whatever the shape's size (0: a share of the shape, set by Bank width).
Cut the bank into this many flat terraces stepping down to the water, as real heights the sun lights (a lit top, a shaded riser), counted from the waterline this stroke leaves. 0: the plain bank.
Width of one layer, ledge and riser together: Shore layers times this is how far the terraces reach inland.
Height of each step. 0 shares the bank's whole rise out between the layers, so the last one meets the plain.
How much of each layer is flat ledge; the rest is the riser, which the sun shades.
How far the layer edges wander, so neighboring risers meet and part and no two layers run parallel for long.
Contour: the layers follow the shoreline. Circular: many round bites cut out of the bank, layer after layer, each step a scalloped arc (retail lava-2).
Width of the whole curve, foot to top, kept the same whatever the brush size (0: a share of the brush set by Slope softness).
Cut the face into this many flat ledges with risers between them.
How much of each step is flat; the rest is the riser.
How much riser positions and step heights wander along the outline.
How many stretches of the terraces lose their shelf, so the steps no longer run unbroken round the shape (100: most stretches lose it, and short ledges survive). 0 keeps the terraces whole.
The height of the crest, in height units. The section canvas marks the plain (the map's base height) and the sea. Combine decides what the landform does to the ground it meets.
Raise to keeps the higher of the ground and the landform. Cut to keeps the lower. Flatten to sets the ground to the landform wherever it reaches, up or down.
How far the section strays sideways from the path you drew, in waves as long as the Variation size.
How much the section widens and narrows along the path (100: from half to twice its width).
How far the surface rises and falls, in height units, in waves as long as the Variation size. It is zero at the feet.
The wavelength of the wander and of the width and height variation.
How much of the variation acts at the foot of the section (100: all of it, 0: none, 200: twice). It blends into the next one up to the middle of the section.
How much of the variation acts from the middle of the section to its crest. Set the foot to 0 and this to 200 for variation that grows toward the crest.
Tapering spurs that branch off this ridge (off a crater, its rim), grown from the shape's own seed. Each joins its parent at the crest.
Average reach of a spur; each runs from about half to one and a half times this.
0: spurs leave swept back at about 40 degrees (off a crater, straight out); 100: scattered up to square and beyond, and more winding.
A spur's width at its root, as a share of the ridge's own (a crater's radius, on a crater); it flares a little where it joins.
How much a spur narrows and lowers toward its tip.
A spur's root height as a share of the ridge's crest (of the crater's rim height).
The share of spurs that fork once, two thirds of the way out, into a shorter spur.
Swells the outer half of every spur into a rounded lobe, so it ends in a knuckle, not a point.
Jagged crest: its height drops in and out along the ridge (the peaks keep full height); on a crater, its spurs.
The ridge swells and shrinks, wider and lower in places, along its path (a crater's spurs, on a crater).
The ridge narrows and lowers toward both ends of its path.
How high the rim stands, as a share of the crater's Depth (34% is the usual rim); the bowl floor does not change, so a tall rim needs no deeper bowl.
Split the rim into this many sectors of different height and width (a lopsided ring, not an even one).
How different the sectors are: 0 equal; 100 from a faint low ridge to a tall, broad massif.
Deliberate breaks in the rim, where it sinks to a low saddle.
Angular width of each gap; a wide one leaves an open crescent.
Width of the cut at its widest. The grid is 2 px, so a cut never reads narrower than about 4 px, however thin it is set.
How far the cut zigzags off its path, and how its depth varies along it.
Side cuts that leave the main cut, and fork once, grown from the shape's own seed. Network mode ignores them.
Average reach of a branch; each runs from about half to one and a half times this.
0: branches leave at about 25 degrees to the cut; 100: up to square.
How much the cut narrows and shallows toward its ends and its branch tips.
0: cut along the stroke. 1: a connected polygonal fracture network over the stroke's whole footprint (Diameter sets how far it reaches), as on Red's rock platforms.
Typical width of a block between the cuts.
Raises the world's own crack field along the cut, so the rock beside it breaks up (0 leaves only the cut).
Paints the world's own wet (dark) ground along the cut, so it reads dark whatever the ground (it layers on rock, snow or moss).
Add a band of broken plates on this stroke only. Off preserves the original water shape.
Reach from this stroke's waterline into the water.
Reach from this stroke's waterline onto land, with broken pressure ridges.
Typical width of the interlocking polygonal plates.
Flat water plates sit this high above sea; land keeps its existing height. Rock slabs: how far the land slabs stand above their seams.
Plate material (1 rock slabs, 2 frost crystals)

2: frost crystals, parallel straight needles in patches of three directions, cut by straight seams, thinning toward deep water (Plate size is the patch, Plate gap the needle spacing; retail Ice). 1: low flat rock slabs that interlock along the shore with dark seams between them, and a shallow ledge under the water (Crystal). The band follows this stroke's own waterline, so separate shores stay separate.
Frost crystals: the share of patches that carry needles at all; the rest of the band is plain ice. Needles in a patch are also dropped at random, so lines are sparse, fine and of varied length.

Crystals: separate faceted crystals (shards, or big blocks as on Ice). Column mound: a mound tiled with flat polygonal columns (Crystal world). Berg: a rough ice block with an uneven outline, broken corners and rough faces that take the world's own slope relief (Ice); Sides, Width, Height and Variation apply.
Remove the mound incline from each column top so its height steps distinctly from its neighbors.
Sides of each crystal's footprint (crystals form; columns are Voronoi, mostly 5-6 sides).
Crystals: typical base width. Column mound: column top width (retail ~15).
Column mound: how far a column top steps up or down from its neighbors (retail ~16; ~40% flush).
How many crystals a click grows; a longer stroke grows more.
0: pointed; higher cuts the tops level (a flat-topped prism).
How far each apex leans off its base center.
Spread of sizes, heights and side counts.
World default keeps the World panel's Crisp waterline. Hard: the water starts at the shoreline with ragged stairs, as retail draws it. Faded: the water fades in over a few pixels.

World default keeps the World panel's Shallow-to-deep step. Hard: the shallow color stops at one depth with ragged stairs (retail Green). Faded: the color follows the depth ramp gradually (retail Archipelago).

World default keeps the World panel's Lit bed. Lit bed: the ground under the water, lit by the same sun and tinted (retail). Noise water: the earlier flat noise texture. Cracked bed: lit bed over cracked rock-like ground, tinted (Red's shelf shallows).
Berg: 0 turns each block at random, 100 sets its faces square to the shape's frame (four sides then make an axis-aligned box).
Berg: how fast the faces rise, in height units per px (shown in percent: 90% is 0.9 units per px). Each face varies by Outline jitter.
Berg: how far the face angles, distances and steepness stray from a regular polygon, and how much each face wavers along its length.
Berg: extra planes of their own steepness that cut corners off the block.
Berg: fractal roughness added to the height, from 40 px lumps to 4 px grain.
Berg: the slope of the ramp that brings the top down away from the Tilt direction (the top is level toward it, at Height).
Level top toward the tilt (berg, share of radius)
Berg: how far from the center, toward the tilt direction, the top stays level before it ramps down (negative: the ramp starts on the far side of the center).
Berg: the direction the top rises toward, turning with the shape's frame.

What the brush paints. Denser scatter supplies its own stones where the World panel's Boulders and Debris are 0 and multiplies them where they are not. Style settings go more or less than the world's own value; Strength is how far. Erase clears every mask and style under the brush.
Also paint a mask over the shape's own footprint, strongest where the shape is (a rocky mesa, a mossy hill).
How fully the shape paints its mask.
Relief (ribs, lumps) inside the shape: below 0 smoother, above 0 stronger, up to 4x.
Cracks inside the shape: below 0 fewer, above 0 more (also where the world has none).
Contour banding inside the shape: below 0 fainter, above 0 stronger (also where the world has none).
Share of rock on steep faces inside the shape: below 0 more grass and moss, above 0 more rock.
Erosion rate inside the shape (the GPU pass), times 1 + this: below 0 less, above 0 more, -100% none.
Sand and scree inside the shape, times 1 + this: below 0 less, above 0 more.
Grass and moss cover inside the shape, times 1 + this: below 0 more bare rock, above 0 more cover.
Where rock shows inside the shape, times 1 + this: below 0 less, above 0 more.
Column mound: tilts each column's top into one or two planes that meet at a crease, so the tops read as crumpled multi-facet crystal, not flat plates. 0 keeps flat tops.
Column mound: the mound mixes three column widths (Column width, about half and about a third of it), the small ones where the mound is highest and in patches. 0 keeps one width.
Column mound: the share of the widest columns (and some of the middle ones) left as smooth hill with no flat top, taking the world's hill relief. 0 tiles the whole mound.

Crater: tiles the bowl, rim and apron with polygonal facets (planes fitted to the crater's own surface, stepped a few units from each other), so its contours are straight-edged like crystal. 0 keeps the smooth crater.
How far the outline of the foot strays in and out, in lobes of about 20 and 55 px (Painted Desert aprons and mesa feet).
Lumps of this height, 13 to 30 px across, on the apron and the lower face; the level cap and the plain are left alone.
Fingers on the joined coast: length and (less) width of each finger. Fingers never reach past this stroke's bank.
How much each layer's width and riser height change along the shore and from one layer to the next, so risers bunch, part and merge as retail's do. 0 keeps the even layers.
Circular layers: the typical radius of the round bites cut from the bank.
Crater facets: the width of each polygonal facet. 0 sizes them by the crater's radius (about a third of it, 14-36 px); retail's crater walls break into cells of 12-20 px.

Crater facets: how far each facet may stand above or below the crater's own surface, in height units either way (shown in tenths: 3 is the earlier ragged crater). Retail's crater walls are smooth planes broken by a thin web, so a small step keeps the sun's light running smoothly across the wall.

Crater facets: 100 marks the whole crater as one crystal skin (no seams in the crystal field) and leaves the thin web between the facets to the shader (World knobs crystalCraterWeb and its relatives), drawn at pixel size so its lines run thin and wander; 0 inks each facet's seam in the field as before.
Rock slab variety (share of slabs broken into fine mesh)

Rock slabs (Plate material 1): in patches, a slab breaks into a fine mesh of cells about 0.4 of Plate size inside its own outline, so the large seams stay. This sets the share of slabs that break; 0 keeps every slab whole.
Rock slabs: the crystal-field value of a seam. 50 is the earlier black seam; higher values thin it (the shader inks only below 66) toward the hairline seams of retail's shore band.

Ice: breaks part of the mountain into angular facets: tilted planes fitted to the mountain's own surface, a little steeper, stepped a few units off their neighbors and partly buried where the ground rises past them. They share the mountain's material and light, so they stand out of the snow as part of it. 0 keeps the smooth mountain.
Ice facets: the typical width of one facet.

How far the hill's whole outline, crest to foot, strays in and out in lobes of about half, a fifth and a fourteenth of its radius, so it folds like a retail lunar formation instead of an oval. 0 keeps the smooth outline.

Circular layers: how much the bites differ from one another, in radius (a few large among many small), in the spacing of their rings, and in how many sites keep one, so they gather in clusters with bare stretches, as retail lava-2's do. 0: the even circles.
Contour layers: extra spread in layer width along the shore, on top of Layer width variation (100 is about 2.7 times between the narrowest and the widest). 0: none.
KNOBS: Light from the south (0: due west)
Painted sand to the crown (sand bars)
Order (0 scattered, ink cracks; 1 beds, joints, lit relief cracks)
Beds and joints from slope (painted rock always)
Bed thickness (px along the ground, or height units)
Beds spaced by height (0 px along the ground)
Bed tilt (height per px; 2 north: level rows)
Joint and gully lean from north-south (deg)
Lit bed under shallow water (0 noise water)
Bed light carried through the tint
Rock tile blotch contrast (1 as drawn, 0 flat)
Rock relief lit on walls that face the viewer (0: world-space look)
Rock glints kept outside painted rock
Beds on the contours, joints down the fall line (0 fixed screen directions)
Wide fall line radius, level ground under rock (px)
Slope under which structure fades into broken rock
Bed riser height (units; 0 the bed's own)
Beds follow the smoothed ground (0 the grid's own bumps)
Joints offset from bed to bed (share of spacing)
Third, finer facet level (share of tilt)
Bed lit by its own relief only
Direction wander (share of a half turn)
Dark crease at each step foot, any facing
Shine only on slopes above (0: everywhere)
Roughness only on raised ground and slopes
Dim the body between glints (near-white surface)
Dark pits on raised ground and slopes
Darker where turned from the sun
Melt pockets: share of cells at the coast
Melt pockets: reach inland (share of the band)
Melt pockets: depth below the sea

HELP.plateau: Paint a level crest above the height where this stroke begins. New strokes can build on top.
HELP.hill: Paint a rounded ridge along any path. A later stroke adds more height to the existing ground.
HELP.mountain: Paint a narrower, peaked ridge. New strokes add to the existing height, without a flat summit.
HELP.ramp: Draw between terrain levels. A smooth center joins the endpoint heights with rounded approaches; shoulder roughness stays outside the route. Longer paths make gentler grades.
HELP.deep: Guide a deep channel. Coast freedom varies the banks; Automatic shallows controls extra shelves. The center stays deep until you paint over it.
HELP.shallow: Set the bed 7 below sea level. Paint through deep water to make a shallow passage, or through land to make shallows.
HELP.smooth: Blend the starting surface toward its local average. Repeat a new stroke for more smoothing.
HELP.lower: Lower the starting surface by the chosen amount. New strokes can dig farther.
HELP.offset: Paint an area to raise or lower by the chosen height. Its edge is natural and its softness sets cliff or slope; the ground keeps its own relief.
HELP.crystal: Grow a cluster of faceted crystals along the stroke: their sides, size, count, how flat their tops are and how much they lean are brush options. Height sets the tallest.
HELP.sand: Paint sand cover: the ground under the brush becomes sand (on slopes too, so a hill set in sand has sandy feet). Heights do not change.
HELP.grass: Paint ground cover: clears sand (painted or weathered) back to the world's own ground, such as grass. Heights do not change.
HELP.paint: Paint a material over the ground, or a scatter density: rock showing through, snow or ice, wet (dark) ground and moss take the world's own materials; denser or sparser scatter multiplies the World panel's Boulders and Debris (at 0 nothing shows). Strength is how fully it paints, Softness the edge. Heights do not change.
HELP.fissure: Cut a fissure along the stroke, or (Mode 1) a network of cuts over its footprint. Branches, jaggedness, width and depth are brush options; the world's own crack field is raised along the cut.
HELP.erase: Paint plain ground: hills, water, craters, cracks, painted masks and style under the brush return to the dry base level, with a natural edge.
HELP.crater: Strike a crater: a bowl below the ground where you click, a raised rim and a fading apron. Drag for an elongated crater.
HELP.move: Drag to move · Shift + drag for height · Shift snaps rotate / scale · P: path · V: transform · arrows: nudge · Shift F: focus canvas
HELP.landform: Draw a landform along a path: the path is the crest, and the section across it is one curve you shape on both sides. The crest stands at an elevation you set, and the ground is raised to it, cut down to it or flattened to it. A second curve sets the crest's height along the path.
